The seminar hall at the engineering college held sixty first-years, and Naveen, a final-year, had been invited to talk about his summer internship. He clicked to his first slide. "So basically we built an ETL pipeline feeding an LLM with RAG, deployed on K8s, with CI/CD for the MLOps side."
In the third row, Suraj stopped writing. Around Suraj, pens paused. Someone opened a phone under the desk.
Naveen kept going, faster, pleased with how smoothly it was flowing. "Obviously the latency on the vector DB was the bottleneck."
By minute four, half the hall was looking at the ceiling fans.
At the end there were no questions. Naveen walked out a little annoyed. "Tough crowd," he told the coordinator. "I kept it really basic."

qa.q: How many first-years were in the seminar hall?
qa.a: Sixty first-years.

qa.q: Why did Naveen feel he had kept it really basic?
qa.a: Naveen felt pleased with how smoothly it flowed because those terms were everyday words in his internship, so they seemed basic to him and he couldn't see that first-years had never heard them.

qa.q: What could Naveen have done in his first minute instead?
qa.a: Say in plain words what the project did, with one everyday example, and explain any acronym he truly needed before using it.

qa.q: What was the talk like for Suraj in the third row?
qa.a: Suraj stopped writing almost immediately, likely feeling lost and maybe a bit resentful at being made to feel behind.

grounding: It shows a student presenter assuming first-years know his acronyms and losing them within the first minute.

Hi Anjali,
Today's outreach talk at the girls' school was a disaster, and honestly I don't know what more I could have done. I spent two weeks on the slides! I opened with how CRISPR-Cas9 uses a guide RNA to find a PAM site, then went straight into off-target effects and HDR versus NHEJ. Standard stuff, it's in every first-year module.
Within a minute the Class 9 students were whispering and one was drawing on her hand. Their teacher kept smiling at me in a tight way. When I asked "Any questions?", one girl said, "What's a gene?" A gene! I nearly laughed.
I think they just weren't interested in science. Should I even bother going back next month?
Elizabeth

qa.q: What did one girl ask when Elizabeth asked for questions?
qa.a: "What's a gene?"

qa.q: Why does Elizabeth think the students just weren't interested in science?
qa.a: The terms feel standard to Elizabeth after a first-year module, so the whispering looks like boredom rather than students lost from the first slide.

qa.q: What should Elizabeth change before going back next month?
qa.a: Start with what a gene is, use a simple picture like editing one word in a recipe, and leave out acronyms unless each one is explained.

qa.q: What might the teacher's tight smile have meant?
qa.a: The teacher may have seen the class was lost from the start and felt uncomfortable, wanting to be polite to the visitor while the lesson wasn't landing.

grounding: It shows a student presenter assuming school students know the acronyms and background and losing them at once.

passage: Manoj, you missed my film club talk, so let me, Dhruv, tell you how it went. I had fifteen minutes to pitch our short film to the funding committee. First line: "We'll shoot 4K log at twenty-four fps, with a thirty-five mil prime and a gimbal for the oners." I thought that sounded professional. The committee is two economics professors and the canteen manager. Within a minute the canteen manager was checking his watch. One professor asked, "Sorry, what's a oner?" I explained it with more terms. She nodded slowly, the way people nod when they've given up. We got half the money we asked for. I was annoyed at them for days. But I've been thinking... maybe I never told them what the film was even about.

qa.q: Who was on the funding committee?
qa.a: Two economics professors and the canteen manager.

qa.q: Why was Dhruv annoyed at the committee for days?
qa.a: Dhruv thought the talk sounded professional and clear, so the poor result felt like the committee's fault; only later did it occur to Dhruv that they never heard what the film was about.

qa.q: How could Dhruv open the pitch next time?
qa.a: Start with the story of the film and why it matters, in plain words, and bring in camera details only if someone asks.

qa.q: How might the professor have felt asking "What's a oner?"
qa.a: She might have felt a little awkward admitting she didn't know, and when the answer used more terms, she gave up trying to follow.

grounding: It shows a student presenter assuming a committee knows film terms and losing them in the first minute.

I'm Gurleen, and I was in the second row for the NSS orientation when Nilesh, our final-year volunteer lead, gave his talk to about eighty first-years.
He opened with: "So this term we continue the WASH audit in Khanpur, finish the DPR, and hand the O&M plan to the SHG as per the SBM guidelines."
I watched the faces around me. The boy next to me looked at his friend. A girl in front wrote "DPR??" in her notebook. Within a minute, three people were on their phones.
Nilesh kept going, faster, clicking through slides of charts. When someone at the back finally asked, "Sorry, what does WASH mean?", he paused and said, a bit sharply, "It's on the first slide," though it wasn't.
Afterwards he told me, "Nobody here even cares." I'm not sure that was true. They just didn't know what he was talking about.

qa.q: What did the girl in front write in her notebook?
qa.a: She wrote "DPR??" in her notebook.

qa.q: What does Nilesh's sharp reply and his comment afterwards suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He seemed irritated and resentful, blaming the first-years for not caring, because the acronyms were so familiar to him that he didn't see he had lost them.

qa.q: What went wrong in the first minute, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: He started with acronyms nobody knew; he could open with one plain story of what the volunteers actually did in Khanpur and explain each short form the first time.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see the first-years' reaction differently from Nilesh?
qa.a: Gurleen thinks they weren't bored or uncaring; they simply didn't understand the words, which is why they drifted to their phones.

grounding: It shows a student presenter assuming first-years know the acronyms and background, and losing them in the first minute.

Monday: Siddharth, twenty-one, rehearsed his final-year project talk for Pradeep in the hostel room. "Our CNN hits an F1 of 0.91 on the augmented set, beating the baseline SVM." Pradeep, a history student, asked, "What's an F1?" Siddharth laughed. "Don't worry, the panel will know."
Thursday: The panel had three members. One was the dean of humanities. By the second slide, the dean was frowning at the screen; by the fourth, writing something in the margin. When she asked, "What problem does this solve for a farmer?", Siddharth said, "As I said, the F1 is 0.91," and moved on.
Next Monday: The feedback sheet said "strong technical work, unclear to non-specialists". Siddharth threw it on his bed. "They should have sent a real panel." Then he picked it up again and read the line about farmers twice.

qa.q: What did the feedback sheet say?
qa.a: It said "strong technical work, unclear to non-specialists".

qa.q: Why does Siddharth feel resentful about the feedback?
qa.a: He was so sure his terms were common knowledge that the panel's confusion feels like their failing, not a gap in how he explained it.

qa.q: At which point could Siddharth have caught the problem early, and what would help?
qa.a: On Monday, when Pradeep asked what an F1 was; he could have treated that question as a warning and opened with the farmer's problem in plain words.

qa.q: What was the presentation like for the dean of humanities?
qa.a: The dean was probably lost from the second slide and frustrated when her direct question about farmers got a number instead of an answer.

grounding: It shows a student presenter assuming the panel knows the acronyms and background, losing them early, and resenting the result.

Faculty note, department seminar, 18 September.
Tushar, a final-year student, presented his water-quality project to the first-year batch today. His first slide read: "BOD, COD and TDS trends vs. WQI across three STPs." He began reading it at speed. Within a minute I saw phones come out in the back rows. Kishore, a first-year sitting near me, whispered to a neighbour, "What's an STP?" Tushar kept going, sure the slides were clear. At question time there were no questions. He looked irritated and said the batch "clearly didn't prepare". Afterwards I asked him how many of those terms he had known in his own first year. He was quiet, then said, "None." We agreed he'll rework the first three slides with plain words and one picture of a sewage plant, and present again next week.

qa.a: Kishore whispered, 'What's an STP?'

qa.q: Why did Tushar say the batch clearly didn't prepare?
qa.a: Tushar felt irritated and a little resentful, because the terms were so familiar to him that he assumed they were clear to everyone.

qa.q: What will Tushar change before presenting again, and why?
qa.a: He will rework the first three slides with plain words and a picture of a sewage plant, so first-years can follow from the start.

qa.q: What was the talk like for Kishore and the other first-years?
qa.a: They were lost within a minute, puzzled by short forms nobody explained, so phones came out and no one asked questions.

Saturday night.
Today's talk at the community centre was a disaster and I'm still annoyed, mostly at myself. I'd been asked to explain our college survey on screen time to the mothers' group. I opened with "So our N was 240, and the correlation with self-reported sleep quality was moderate, not causal." Rajni aunty, in the front row, smiled politely. Nobody else moved. I kept going: p-values, sampling, Likert scales. By minute two a baby was crying and two women were chatting in Kannada. My face burned and I thought, they're not even trying. Then Rajni aunty asked, very gently, "Beta, so should my son keep his phone out of his room or not?" That was the whole point, and I hadn't said it once.
Next time: start with her question.
Nazia

qa.q: Where did Nazia give the talk?
qa.a: Nazia gave the talk at the community centre, to the mothers' group.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling during the talk, and why did it go wrong?
qa.a: Nazia felt embarrassed and annoyed, even thinking the audience wasn't trying, because terms like p-values felt normal to Nazia but meant nothing to the listeners.

qa.q: What does Nazia plan for next time, and why is it a good fix?
qa.a: To start with Rajni aunty's question, the practical point the listeners care about, before any statistics.

qa.q: How did Rajni aunty experience the talk?
qa.a: Rajni aunty sat politely through the jargon, then gently asked the simple question the whole talk should have answered.

grounding: Shows a student presenter using research terms the audience doesn't know, losing them within minutes and feeling resentful.

passage: At the gram panchayat hall in Sangole, Yash, a third-year agriculture student, stood up to present his project on soil health to fifty farmers. He had rehearsed it perfectly for his professors. "Namaskar. So, the soil test shows low NPK and poor CEC, so we recommend IPM plus site-specific nutrient management, with FYM and bio-fertilisers per the SHC." He looked up. Blank faces. Someone's phone rang. An old farmer at the back said, "Beta, what is NPK?" Yash blinked. Everyone in his college knew NPK. He tried again, faster. Two farmers left for tea. Lakshmi, a farmer who ran the women's group, raised her hand. "Tell us what to put in the field, in our words." Yash stood there, face hot. He had lost the room within a minute and hadn't even noticed.

qa.q: How many farmers did Yash present to?
qa.a: Fifty farmers.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when the old farmer asked what NPK was?
qa.a: He felt surprised and flustered, because everyone in his college knew NPK and he hadn't thought the farmers might not.

qa.q: What could Yash do to reach the farmers?
qa.a: Use their words and examples, explaining what to put in the field without acronyms, as Lakshmi asked.

qa.q: How did the farmers experience the start of Yash's talk?
qa.a: They felt lost and bored, with blank faces, a phone ringing and two leaving for tea.

grounding: Shows a student presenter using acronyms the audience doesn't know and losing them in the first minute.

passage: In the seminar room at the university in Manchester, Chidi stood up to present his research to the first-year students. It was his favourite topic. "Right, so our RCT used a DiD approach with FE at the district level, and we clustered SEs to handle ICC. The ATE was significant." He clicked to the next slide. Valentina, in the front row, had stopped writing after the second word. Around her, people were checking their phones. Chidi didn't notice. He was already on the next slide. At the end, the tutor asked if anyone had questions. Silence. Afterwards, Valentina told him, kindly, "It sounded brilliant. I just didn't understand one word after 'Right, so.'" Chidi looked at his slides. Every term had felt as normal as breathing. He had forgotten that he had once needed them explained too.

qa.q: When did Valentina stop writing?
qa.a: After the second word.

qa.q: What was Chidi feeling when Valentina spoke to him afterwards?
qa.a: He felt surprised and a bit embarrassed, seeing that terms that felt normal to him meant nothing to his audience.

qa.q: What could Chidi change for his next presentation?

qa.q: What was the seminar like for Valentina?

Nilesh,
You asked how my talk for the first-years went. Badly, and it's my fault.
I had ten minutes on our robotics project. I opened with: "So we used a PID loop on the BLDC motors, tuned with IMU feedback over I2C." I thought that was the simple version. In the first row, a girl wrote PID in her notebook with a big question mark next to it. By minute two, half the room was on their phones.

Next month I'm giving it again. This time I'm starting with a video of the robot falling over, and explaining why it falls.
Saurabh

Kunal, you know I started tutoring the first-year stats batch? I'm Vandana, by the way, in case your podcast needs names.
So, first class, I walked in and said, "Right, hypothesis testing: null, alternative, p-value, reject or fail to reject." Wrote it all on the board in two minutes. Thirty blank faces.
My first thought, honestly, was: did they not do the reading? Then one student said, "Ma'am, what's a hypothesis?" Ma'am! I'm twenty. And I'd skipped the one word everything else sits on.
That night I asked my mother to explain her office's insurance form to me, with all the jargon. By the third term I was lost and cross with her. That's what I'd done to thirty people.
Now I start every class with a coin and a question: is this coin fair? We spend ten minutes arguing before I say a single technical word.

qa.a: One student asked, 'Ma'am, what's a hypothesis?'

qa.q: What was Vandana's first thought when faced with thirty blank faces?
qa.a: Vandana felt irritated and puzzled, wondering whether the students had skipped the reading, because the terms seemed basic.

qa.q: How does Vandana now open each class, and why does it help?
qa.a: With a coin and the question 'is this coin fair?', letting students argue before any technical words, so they build the idea first.

qa.q: What might the first class have been like for the students?
qa.a: They were probably confused and anxious, facing terms they'd never met, until one brave student asked what a hypothesis was.

Monday. Pankaj rehearsed his internship pitch for the water project's village meeting in front of the mirror: "Our intervention optimises groundwater recharge via check dams, improving the aquifer's yield indicators." It sounded professional. He was sure it was clear.
Wednesday. He tried it on Arohi, who studies literature. She stopped him after one sentence. "What's an aquifer? What's recharge? Who are you talking to?" For a moment he felt annoyed. Everyone knows what an aquifer is. Then he remembered he had learned the word only last semester.
Saturday. At the meeting under the banyan tree, Pankaj held up a bucket with a hole in it and a sponge. "The rain runs away like this. The small dam holds it so the ground can drink, like this sponge. Your wells stay full longer."
An old farmer nodded. "So it's a pond that feeds the well."
"Exactly," Pankaj said.

qa.q: What does Arohi study?
qa.a: Arohi studies literature.

qa.q: Why was Pankaj annoyed for a moment on Wednesday?
qa.a: Pankaj felt irritated because aquifer seemed like a word everyone knows, until remembering it had been learned only last semester.

qa.q: What made the Saturday version work?
qa.a: Using a bucket, a sponge and plain words about wells turned the jargon into something the farmers could see.

qa.q: How does the old farmer understand the idea?
qa.a: The farmer puts it in plain words, a pond that feeds the well, which shows the new version landed.

grounding: Shows a student presenter who assumes his audience knows the technical background, then rebuilds the talk from a beginner's view.
